chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Al-A'ala ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the nose is cut from the soft part, the complete blood-money is due for it; and for the teeth of the man, the complete blood-money is due; and for his two ears, the complete blood-money is due; and the two feet and the two eyes are in that same status.

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Blood-money or financial compensation for injury or death
key_terms.الْمَارِنِ: The soft, fleshy part of the nose

ai.seo_question: What injuries require the complete blood-money (diyah) according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the legal principle of 'tammah' (completeness) for specific limbs, affirming that the loss of the nose, teeth, ears, feet, and eyes triggers the full blood-money (diyah) rather than a partial amount. In Shia jurisprudence, this serves as a primary textual basis for categorizing these distinct body parts as having independent value, distinguishing them from other injuries that might only warrant a fraction of the compensation. The narration underscores the precision of Imami fiqh in quantifying bodily integrity, reflecting the broader theological emphasis on the sanctity of the human form as a trust from God.
